text.en: Named after Quetzalcoatl, the feathered-serpent god of the Aztecs; northropi honours aircraft designer Jack Northrop

diet.note: Witton and Naish (2008) argue azhdarchids were stork-like ground foragers eating small animals and carrion; Lehman (reported by UT News 2021) and the NPS describe it probing water and mud for invertebrates.

timeRange.note: Maastrichtian (Javelina Formation). Ages are ICS Maastrichtian stage bounds from PBDB occurrences; popular sources give about 67 Ma (Field Museum) or about 70 Ma (UT News).

wingspanM.note: About 10 m (Witton & Naish 2008); 10–11 m (Witton & Habib 2010); 36–39 ft, about 11.0–11.9 m (NPS). Larger spans of 11–12 m and 15.5 m appear in Witton & Naish (2008) only as Langston's scenarios for mass estimates, not as measurements.

text.en: Quetzalcoatlus was a giant pterosaur, a flying reptile, not a dinosaur. With wings about 10 metres across, it was among the largest animals ever known to fly. Its fossils come from Big Bend National Park in Texas, from the very end of the Cretaceous. Scientists still debate how it fed: stalking small animals on land, or probing for crabs and worms in shallow water.
The first fossil, a wing bone, was found in 1971 in Big Bend National Park, Texas, by Douglas Lawson, then a University of Texas student.

uncertain.note: No verified mass estimate specific to Q. northropi; Witton & Naish (2008) cite earlier estimates of 86–136 kg and give about 250 kg for a generic 10 m azhdarchid.
How azhdarchids fed is debated: stork-like ground foraging (Witton & Naish 2008) versus probing water and mud for invertebrates (Lehman, reported by UT News 2021; NPS).
